item.title: “Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless. What five? The…
item.description:
“Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless. What five? The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of peril, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world. These five perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.61

item.title: The foolish, ignorant person delights in heedlessness, But the wise one guards heedlessness as his greatest treasure. Do not yield to heedlessness, do not yield…
item.description:
The foolish, ignorant person delights in heedlessness,
But the wise one guards heedlessness as his greatest treasure.
Do not yield to heedlessness, do not yield to sensual pleasures.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 86 – Aṅgulimālasutta

item.title: All conditioned things are truly impermanent, They arise and then pass away — Their nature is always thus. They come into being, Then they again…
item.description:
All conditioned things are truly impermanent,
They arise and then pass away —
Their nature is always thus.
They come into being,
Then they again are destroyed.
Blissful indeed when they
Are calmed and at peace.

From: Dīgha Nikāya 17 – Mahāsudassanasutta

item.title: - “Lust, Venerable Bharadvāja, is the mind. Sometimes, even toward those who are like mothers, lust arises. Toward those like sisters, lust arises. Toward those…
item.description:
- “Lust, Venerable Bharadvāja, is the mind. Sometimes, even toward those who are like mothers, lust arises. Toward those like sisters, lust arises. Toward those like daughters, lust arises. Bharadvāja, is there another cause, another reason why these young monks … live the holy life completely?” - “Great king, the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has said: ‘Come, monks, contemplate this body from the soles of the feet upward, from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin and full of various impurities. In this body there are: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, intestinal mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, skin oil, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’ This, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks live the perfectly pure holy life for their whole life, completing it fully.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.127

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as lack of clear comprehension. For…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as lack of clear comprehension. For one lacking clear comprehension, monks, unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.68

item.title: Four wheels, nine doors, Full of defilement, tied by greed — Mired in mud, O great hero, What will be the future state Of such…
item.description:
Four wheels, nine doors,
Full of defilement, tied by greed —
Mired in mud,
O great hero,
What will be the future state
Of such a human birth?

(The Blessed One):
Having cut off delight and bondage,
Sensual desire and evil,
Having destroyed the root of craving —
Such will be his future state.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.28
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, through lust, one is not freed. Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form…
item.description:
“Monks, through lust, one is not freed. Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Through lust for feeling … for perception … for formations, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With formations as its object, with formations as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Monks, if anyone says: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will show the coming and going, the passing away and arising, the growth, increase, and expansion of consciousness’ — such a thing is not possible. Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the form element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. If a monk has abandoned lust for the feeling element … for the perception element … for the formation element … Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the consciousness element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. Without that support, consciousness does not expand, does not generate activity, and is liberated. Being liberated, it is steady; being steady, it is content; being content, it is not agitated; being not agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.53
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point cannot be discerned of beings wandering and roaming on, shrouded by ignorance and bound by…
item.description:
“Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point cannot be discerned of beings wandering and roaming on, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving. Monks, suppose a dog was tied by a leash to a strong post or pillar. If it walks, it walks close to that post or pillar. If it stands, it stands close to that post or pillar. If it sits, it sits close to that post or pillar. If it lies down, it lies down close to that post or pillar. So too, monks, an untaught ordinary person regards form as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ He regards feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ If he walks, he walks close to these five aggregates of clinging. If he stands, he stands close to them. If he sits, he sits close to them. If he lies down, he lies close to them. Therefore, monks, one should constantly reflect on one’s own mind thus: ‘For a long time, this mind has been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion. Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled. Through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.100

item.title: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having personally abandoned discontent and aroused satisfaction, on that occasion recited this verse: I abandon pleasure and displeasure, All household thoughts,…
item.description:
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having personally abandoned discontent and aroused satisfaction, on that occasion recited this verse:

I abandon pleasure and displeasure,
All household thoughts,
Making no place anywhere
That could become a basis for sensual desire.
One who has escaped the forest of greed,
Escaped all sensual desire,
Free from greed, not clinging —
He is truly called a monk.
Whatever earth element, space element,
All the form realm in the world —
All things are subject to change,
All things are impermanent.
Whoever understands this,
His conduct is true.
Beings are always attached
To various attachments —
To what they see, hear,
Smell, taste, touch.
Whoever abandons desire here,
With mind undefiled,
Not clinging here or there —
He is called a sage (muni).
Concerning the sixty views
Belonging to wrong thoughts —
Worldlings cling to them,
Grasp and cling.
The monk who has no defilements,
Speaks no evil words,
Clear-minded, always concentrated,
Without deceit, careful —
Escaped from all craving.
The sage who has attained
The peaceful state of Nibbāna,
Awaiting the time of his end,
With mind perfectly still,
Serenely passes into Nibbāna.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 8.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, having heard Brahmā’s request, out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. With the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little…
item.description:
“Monks, having heard Brahmā’s request, out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. With the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some hard to teach, and a few who saw the danger in rebirth to another world and the danger of faulty actions. Just as in a blue lotus pond, a red lotus pond, or a white lotus pond, some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and do not rise above the water, being nourished underwater; some are born in the water, grow in the water, and reach the water’s surface; some are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise up above the water, not wetted by the water.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
